claim: In placebo hypoalgesia research, the strength of treatment expectations and experiences are key components.
source: In placebo hypoalgesia research, the strength of treatment expectations and experiences are key components.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established understanding in the field.

claim: The reliability or precision of expectations had been mostly ignored although being a likely source for interindividual differences.
source: However, the reliability or precision of expectations had been mostly ignored although being a likely source for interindividual differences.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of prior research and a hypothesis about interindividual differences.

claim: Bayesian framework naturally combines expectation magnitudes and precisions.
source: In the present study, we adopted a Bayesian framework, naturally combining expectation magnitudes and precisions.
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework adopted in the study.

claim: Expectations (prior) are integrated with incoming nociceptive information (likelihood) and both are weighted by their relative precision to form the pain percept and placebo effect.
source: This postulates that expectations (prior) are integrated with incoming nociceptive information (likelihood) and both are weighted by their relative precision to form the pain percept and placebo effect.
evidence: This is the theoretical postulate of the Bayesian framework being tested.

claim: Sixty-two healthy subjects received heat pain during fMRI.
source: Sixty-two healthy subjects received heat pain during fMRI.
evidence: This describes the experimental sample and procedure.

claim: Placebo effects were more pronounced in subjects with more precise treatment expectations.
source: Placebo effects were more pronounced in subjects with more precise treatment expectations and correlated positively with the relative precision of the prior expectation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's behavioral data.

claim: Placebo effects correlated positively with the relative precision of the prior expectation.
source: Placebo effects were more pronounced in subjects with more precise treatment expectations and correlated positively with the relative precision of the prior expectation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's behavioral data.

claim: Neural correlates of expectation precision were observed in the periaqueductal gray.
source: Neural correlates of this precision were observed in the periaqueductal gray and the rostral ventromedial medulla
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data.

claim: Neural correlates of expectation precision were observed in the rostral ventromedial medulla.
source: Neural correlates of this precision were observed in the periaqueductal gray and the rostral ventromedial medulla
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data.

claim: Already at the level of the brainstem the precision of an expectation can influence pain perception.
source: indicating that already at the level of the brainstem the precision of an expectation can influence pain perception
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings showing PAG and RVM involvement.

claim: The findings present strong evidence for Bayesian integration in placebo hypoalgesia.
source: presenting strong evidence for Bayesian integration in placebo hypoalgesia.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their combined behavioral and neural findings.

claim: Placebo effects and concomitant hypoalgesia in the pain context exemplify the substantial influence that expectation and experience can have on treatment outcomes.
source: Placebo effects and concomitant hypoalgesia in the pain context exemplify the substantial influence that expectation and experience can have on treatment outcomes and have therefore been intensely investigated over the last decades (Atlas et al., 2010; Colloca and Benedetti, 2006; de la Fuente-Fernández et al., 2001; Enck et al., 2013; Kirsch, 1999; Reicherts et al., 2016; Rief et al., 2011; Schenk et al., 2014; Stone et al., 2005; Wager et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Various studies have identified factors that modulate placebo effects such as value.
source: Various studies have identified factors that modulate these effects such as value (Geuter et al., 2013; Waber et al., 2008), treatment history (Kessner et al., 2014; Kessner et al., 2013), doctor-patient relationship (Benedetti, 2013), and context effects (Blasi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Various studies have identified factors that modulate placebo effects such as treatment history.
source: Various studies have identified factors that modulate these effects such as value (Geuter et al., 2013; Waber et al., 2008), treatment history (Kessner et al., 2014; Kessner et al., 2013), doctor-patient relationship (Benedetti, 2013), and context effects (Blasi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Various studies have identified factors that modulate placebo effects such as doctor-patient relationship.
source: Various studies have identified factors that modulate these effects such as value (Geuter et al., 2013; Waber et al., 2008), treatment history (Kessner et al., 2014; Kessner et al., 2013), doctor-patient relationship (Benedetti, 2013), and context effects (Blasi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Various studies have identified factors that modulate placebo effects such as context effects.
source: Various studies have identified factors that modulate these effects such as value (Geuter et al., 2013; Waber et al., 2008), treatment history (Kessner et al., 2014; Kessner et al., 2013), doctor-patient relationship (Benedetti, 2013), and context effects (Blasi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: These modulators are likely to affect the precision or inverse variance of expectations.
source: Importantly, these modulators are likely to affect the precision or inverse variance of those expectations, which might explain – at least in part – the large interindividual differences observed in placebo hypoalgesia studies (Vase et al., 2009; Wager et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how known modulators might work, supported by citations about interindividual differences.

claim: Large interindividual differences are observed in placebo hypoalgesia studies.
source: Importantly, these modulators are likely to affect the precision or inverse variance of those expectations, which might explain – at least in part – the large interindividual differences observed in placebo hypoalgesia studies (Vase et al., 2009; Wager et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Different precision levels in expectations and prior treatment experience seem to potentially change treatment outcomes.
source: For that reason, it is presumed that different precision levels in expectations and prior treatment experience seem to potentially change treatment outcomes (Büchel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Pollo and colleagues presented different verbal instructions to manipulate patients' treatment response expectancies and observed the largest analgesic effect in the 'sure treatment' group compared to two other groups being either non-informed or having only a 50% chance of receiving a painkiller.
source: Pollo and colleagues presented different verbal instructions to manipulate patients' treatment response expectancies and observed the largest analgesic effect in the 'sure treatment' group compared to two other groups being either non-informed or having only a 50% chance of receiving a painkiller (Pollo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited prior study.

claim: The manipulation of the probability of treatment is likely to have an effect on the ensuing placebo response.
source: This manipulation of the probability of treatment indicates that this is likely to have an effect on the ensuing placebo response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Pollo et al. study.

claim: The more precise expectations are the more probable a specific treatment outcome might be presumed.
source: The more precise expectations are the more probable a specific treatment outcome might be presumed.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the relationship between precision and probability.

claim: More recent approaches or frameworks in pain research already focused on accounting for several modulating factors influencing pain perception to provide a broader view on this very subjective topic.
source: More recent approaches or frameworks in pain research already focused on accounting for several modulating factors influencing pain perception to provide a broader view on this very subjective topic (Anchisi and Zanon, 2015; Büchel et al., 2014; Petzschner et al., 2017; Wager et al., 2013; Wiech et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent frameworks.

claim: Optimal Bayesian integration is a framework that explicitly accounts for variability of prior information such as expectations.
source: At the heart of this model is optimal Bayesian integration (Knill and Pouget, 2004; Körding and Wolpert, 2004; O'Reilly et al., 2012), a framework that explicitly accounts for variability of prior information such as expectations and might thus be helpful to explain the integration of expectations and sensory information in placebo hypoalgesia (Büchel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bayesian integration literature.

claim: The brain constantly integrates incoming sensory input with expectations and generates new expectations about the environment to minimize future surprise.
source: Implicit in this idea is the assumption, that the brain constantly integrates incoming sensory input with expectations and, as a consequence, generates new expectations about the environment to minimize future surprise (Feldman and Friston, 2010; Friston, 2010; Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption supported by citations to predictive coding literature.

claim: Bayesian integration optimally integrates previous expectations (prior) with incoming sensory information (likelihood) and makes a prediction about the outcome of a certain event (posterior).
source: In essence, Bayesian integration optimally integrates previous expectations (prior) with incoming sensory information (likelihood) and makes a prediction about the outcome of a certain event (posterior): the posterior is proportional to the product of prior and likelihood.
evidence: This is a description of Bayesian integration principles.

claim: In Bayesian integration, both prior and likelihood are weighted by their relative precision to estimate the posterior.
source: Importantly, in this framework, both terms are weighted by their relative precision to estimate the posterior.
evidence: This is a key principle of Bayesian integration.

claim: Previous treatment experience and expectations serve as the Bayesian prior being illustrated by a probability distribution reflecting pain relief as well as treatment efficacy precision.
source: Putting this into the placebo context, previous treatment experience and expectations serve as the Bayesian prior being illustrated by a probability distribution reflecting pain relief as well as treatment efficacy precision.
evidence: This is the application of Bayesian framework to placebo context.

claim: A new incoming untreated pain experience reflects the likelihood distribution.
source: A new incoming untreated pain experience reflects the likelihood distribution.
evidence: This is the application of Bayesian framework to placebo context.

claim: A highly precise prior treatment expectation should lead to a stronger placebo effect as compared to a highly variable expectation.
source: A highly precise prior treatment expectation should lead to a stronger placebo effect as compared to a highly variable expectation.
evidence: This is a prediction from the Bayesian framework.

claim: Numerous imaging studies identified brain regions being involved in processing placebo hypoalgesia.
source: Furthermore, numerous imaging studies identified brain regions being involved in processing placebo hypoalgesia (for a review see Wager and Atlas, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Models that can parsimoniously account for several modulating factors are essential to better understand and relate behavioral as well as neuronal aspects of sensory processing such as pain.
source: Models that can parsimoniously account for several modulating factors (Anchisi and Zanon, 2015; Büchel et al., 2014; Wager et al., 2013; Wiech et al., 2014) are essential to better understand and relate behavioral as well as neuronal aspects of sensory processing such as pain.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for comprehensive models, supported by citations.

claim: Treatment instructions had been identical for both groups.
source: Therefore, treatment instructions had been identical for both groups but the treated painful sensation was manipulated in terms of the precision levels of prior treatment expectation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The treated painful sensation was manipulated in terms of the precision levels of prior treatment expectation.
source: Therefore, treatment instructions had been identical for both groups but the treated painful sensation was manipulated in terms of the precision levels of prior treatment expectation.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: One group experienced the placebo treatment as variable (low treatment precision), whereas the other group experienced it as constant (high treatment precision).
source: Via different temperature variations across trials during a conditioning phase (Figure 1D), one group experienced the placebo treatment as variable (low treatment precision), whereas the other group experienced it as constant (high treatment precision).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The PAG was implicated in processing of the precision of vicarious information in a previous study.
source: This a priori region of interest (ROI) hypothesis was especially based on a previous study that implicated the PAG in processing of the precision of vicarious information (Yoshida et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The PAG was involved in the modulation of expected probability of pain in pain avoidance prediction error coding.
source: Supporting this, another study investigated pain avoidance prediction error coding (Roy et al., 2014) and showed that the PAG, among others, was involved in the modulation of expected probability of pain in this context.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: For the conditioning phase, a main effect of condition (placebo vs. control) was observed (F(2,1172) = 24.55, p<0.001).
source: As expected, for the conditioning phase (Figure 2A), a main effect of condition (placebo vs. control) was observed (F(2,1172) = 24.55, p<0.001) reflecting the two distinct temperatures used for creating the treatment experience.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neither a main effect of group (p=0.963) nor an interaction effect of group and condition (p=0.885) was revealed for the conditioning phase.
source: Neither a main effect of group (p=0.963) nor an interaction effect of group and condition (p=0.885) was revealed indicating that the conditioning procedure did not differ between the two groups.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: Subject-specific standard deviations for placebo conditioning ratings was larger for the LTP compared to the HTP group (LTP 22.46 ± 5.33 vs. HTP 13.63 ± 4.76, t(47) = 6.12, p<0.001).
source: Subject-specific standard deviations for placebo conditioning ratings (Figure 2B) and therefore the variability (i.e. inverse precision) of prior treatment expectations was larger for the LTP compared to the HTP group (LTP 22.46 ± 5.33 vs. HTP 13.63 ± 4.76, t(47) = 6.12, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For the test phase, a main effect of condition was observed (F(2,1172) = 4.49, p<0.001).
source: Concerning the test phase (Figure 2C,D), in which all subjects received identical heat stimuli for both conditions, again, a main effect of condition was observed (F(2,1172) = 4.49, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The interaction between group and condition in the test phase became significant (F(2,1172) = 2.72, p=0.007).
source: This interaction of group and condition became significant (F(2,1172) = 2.72, p=0.007) revealing, as hypothesized, that the HTP group (mean VAS difference of the two conditions 6.95 ± SD 11.31) showed a larger placebo effect than the LTP group (1.16 ± 25.43).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: The HTP group showed a larger placebo effect than the LTP group.
source: This interaction of group and condition became significant (F(2,1172) = 2.72, p=0.007) revealing, as hypothesized, that the HTP group (mean VAS difference of the two conditions 6.95 ± SD 11.31) showed a larger placebo effect than the LTP group (1.16 ± 25.43).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: Levels of prior treatment precision modulate the placebo effect.
source: These results suggest that levels of prior treatment precision modulate the placebo effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: The better explanation of the given data was provided by the Bayesian integration model, reflected in a greater posterior model probability.
source: By using a random effects (RFX) Bayesian model selection approach (Rigoux et al., 2014; Stephan et al., 2009) to estimate the overall posterior model probability across subjects, the better explanation of the given data was provided by the Bayesian integration model, reflected in a greater posterior model probability (Figure 3A and B, see also Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2 for single subject fits).
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian model selection shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The RFX conditional expectations of model probabilities of 0.913 (exceedance probability φ1 ≈ 100%) for the Bayes model compared to 0.087 (exceedance probability φ0 ≈ 0%) for the Null model.
source: The RFX conditional expectations of model probabilities of 0.913 (exceedance probability φ1 ≈ 100%) for the Bayes model compared to 0.087 (exceedance probability φ0 ≈ 0%) for the Null model reflect this result (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayesian model selection shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The model incorporating the variance of treatment expectation performed better than the Null model.
source: This finding indicates that the model incorporating the variance of treatment expectation performed better than the Null model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: 31 subjects showed a Bayes factor (BF10) larger than three in favor of the Bayesian integration model.
source: In more detail, 31 subjects (HTP 17, LTP 14) showed a Bayes factor (BF10) larger than three in favor of the Bayesian integration model (Figure 3A), indicating at least a moderate evidence (Kass and Raftery, 1995; Lee and Wagenmakers, 2013).
evidence: This is a result from individual-level Bayesian model comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Seven subjects showed a Bayes factor (BF01) larger than three in favor of the Null model.
source: Concerning the Null model, seven subjects showed a Bayes factor (BF01) larger than three (HTP 4, LTP 3).
evidence: This is a result from individual-level Bayesian model comparison.

claim: The positive evidence ratio was PER10 = 31/7 = 4.43.
source: This led to a positive evidence ratio of PER10 = 31/7 = 4.43.
evidence: This is a calculated statistic from the model comparison results.

claim: No difference between the groups was observed in terms of model fit.
source: Importantly, no difference between the groups was observed meaning that in both groups, a comparable number of model fits was significantly better described by the Bayesian integration model in contrast to the Null model.
evidence: This is a result from comparing model fits across experimental groups.

claim: Attraction weight was positively correlated with the placebo effect (r = 0.306, p=0.016).
source: Attraction weight was positively correlated with the placebo effect (r = 0.306, p=0.016, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In subjects with higher precision (i.e. less variability) in prior treatment expectation a larger placebo effect magnitude was observed.
source: This positive relationship indicates that in subjects with higher precision (i.e. less variability) in prior treatment expectation a larger placebo effect magnitude was observed, whereas subjects with higher precision for the perceived sensory inputs (likelihood) showed smaller magnitudes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between attraction weight and placebo effect.

claim: Subjects with higher precision for the perceived sensory inputs (likelihood) showed smaller placebo effect magnitudes.
source: This positive relationship indicates that in subjects with higher precision (i.e. less variability) in prior treatment expectation a larger placebo effect magnitude was observed, whereas subjects with higher precision for the perceived sensory inputs (likelihood) showed smaller magnitudes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between attraction weight and placebo effect.

claim: Precision of prior treatment expectation was a significant predictor of placebo effect magnitudes (β = −0.883, t(59) = 3.642, p=0.001).
source: Precision of prior treatment expectation was a significant predictor of placebo effect magnitudes (β = −0.883, t(59) = 3.642, p=0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from multiple linear regression analysis.

claim: Precision of sensory inputs showed a trend effect (β = 0.562, t(59) = 1.842, p=0.070).
source: and precision of sensory inputs showed a trend effect (β = 0.562, t(59) = 1.842, p=0.070).
evidence: This is a statistical result from multiple linear regression analysis.

claim: Higher precision or less variability within individual treatment expectations (prior) compared to perceived sensory inputs (likelihood) leads to greater placebo effects.
source: This suggests that higher precision or less variability within individual treatment expectations (prior) compared to perceived sensory inputs (likelihood) leads to greater placebo effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: Higher BOLD signals in the PAG were related to smaller attraction weight values (r = −0.457).
source: Higher BOLD signals in the PAG were related to smaller attraction weight values (r = −0.457).
evidence: This is a result from fMRI analysis.

claim: The less precise prior treatment expectations are relative to sensory inputs, the stronger the PAG BOLD signal.
source: In other words, the less precise prior treatment expectations are relative to sensory inputs, the stronger the PAG BOLD signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PAG activation pattern.

claim: A cluster in the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) was observed (coordinates [2 -36 -46], kE = 16, t(60) = 4.06, puc <0.001) but was not significant when correcting the p-value for the entire volume.
source: Interestingly, the same contrast also revealed a cluster in the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) but this was not significant when correcting the p-value for the entire volume (coordinates [2 -36 -46], kE = 16, t(60) = 4.06, puc <0.001).
evidence: This is a result from fMRI analysis.

claim: In the RVM, a negative correlation with the relative precision was observed (r = −0.451).
source: Here, also a negative correlation with the relative precision was observed (r = −0.451).
evidence: This is a result from fMRI analysis.

claim: Bayesian integration mechanism in the context of placebo hypoalgesia can account for placebo effects on a behavioral level.
source: Our results provide evidence that a Bayesian integration mechanism in the context of placebo hypoalgesia can account for placebo effects on a behavioral level.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: Key parameters of the Bayesian integration mechanism are represented in the periaqueductal gray (PAG).
source: More importantly, our fMRI data revealed that key parameters of this mechanism are represented in the periaqueductal gray (PAG).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: Placebo effects were smaller in subjects with less precision in their prior treatment experience (higher variability).
source: On the behavioral level, we observed that placebo effects were smaller in subjects with less precision in their prior treatment experience (higher variability) and more pronounced for those who perceived the treatment as more constant (higher precision) relative to the incoming sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings.

claim: Placebo effects were more pronounced for those who perceived the treatment as more constant (higher precision) relative to the incoming sensory stimuli.
source: On the behavioral level, we observed that placebo effects were smaller in subjects with less precision in their prior treatment experience (higher variability) and more pronounced for those who perceived the treatment as more constant (higher precision) relative to the incoming sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings.

claim: The observed placebo effect did not correlate with the simple mean of prior treatment expectations.
source: The observed placebo effect did not correlate with the simple mean of prior treatment expectations which reflects the pain intensity during treatment conditioning.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation analysis results.

claim: The intensity mean of the prior was not able to describe the strength of the placebo effect via a correlative relationship, whereas the precision level of the prior was.
source: This intensity mean of the prior was not able to describe the strength of the placebo effect via a correlative relationship, whereas the precision level of the prior was.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation analysis results.

claim: The framework indicates strong evidence for placebo effects being explained by optimal Bayesian integration.
source: By showing that, we were able to present a framework that indicates strong evidence for placebo effects being explained by optimal Bayesian integration (Anchisi and Zanon, 2015; Büchel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings, supported by citations.

claim: Bayesian integration predicted placebo treatment outcome based on various individual prior and likelihood distributions.
source: Also, our results showed that Bayesian integration predicted placebo treatment outcome based on various individual prior and likelihood distributions.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results.

claim: The framework did not favor high over low prior precision or vice versa and predicted the different cases equally well.
source: The framework did not favor high over low prior precision or vice versa and predicted the different cases equally well.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Placebo effect magnitudes are often highly variable.
source: As placebo effect magnitudes are often highly variable (Vase et al., 2009) our results reflect the usefulness of a Bayesian approach that can account for variable as well as precise prior treatment expectations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A Bayesian approach can account for variable as well as precise prior treatment expectations.
source: As placebo effect magnitudes are often highly variable (Vase et al., 2009) our results reflect the usefulness of a Bayesian approach that can account for variable as well as precise prior treatment expectations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in light of prior research.

claim: In some subjects, the Bayesian integration approach did not describe the treatment outcome significantly better than the Null model.
source: In some subjects, the Bayesian integration approach did not describe the treatment outcome significantly better than the Null model.
evidence: This is a summary of the model comparison results.

claim: Not all individuals may combine information of prior experiences and new sensory inputs in an optimal way.
source: Reasons for that are highly speculative and include, for example, that not all individuals may combine information of prior experiences and new sensory inputs in an optimal way.
evidence: This is speculation about why some subjects did not show Bayesian integration.

claim: The experimental manipulation provides new insights in the modulation of different levels of precision of prior treatment expectations by holding the test phase stimuli constant in both groups.
source: Additionally, the experimental manipulation used in this study provides new insights in the modulation of different levels of precision of prior treatment expectations by holding the test phase stimuli constant in both groups.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the experimental design.

claim: The present study used test phase stimuli matching prior expectations concerning treatment precision levels in the HTP but not in the LTP group.
source: The present study used test phase stimuli matching prior expectations concerning treatment precision levels in the HTP but not in the LTP group as induced by the different conditioning procedures.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The study cannot answer the question whether a modulation of precision levels of the test phase stimuli may influence the placebo effect and pain perception in a different way.
source: However, for that reason, our study cannot answer the question whether a modulation of precision levels of the test phase stimuli may influence the placebo effect and pain perception in a different way.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study design.

claim: The PAG signal change represents relative expectation precision of the Bayesian integration process in a placebo hypoalgesia study.
source: Our fMRI data indicated that the PAG signal change represents relative expectation precision of the Bayesian integration process in a placebo hypoalgesia study.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: The PAG is part of the ascending and descending pain system and is crucial for pain modulation.
source: This brainstem area is part of the ascending and descending pain system and is crucial for pain modulation (Fairhurst et al., 2007), pain avoidance prediction error coding (Roy et al., 2014), and the processing of precision of vicarious information (Yoshida et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The PAG is known to mediate pain inhibition.
source: The PAG is not only known to mediate pain inhibition (Jones and Gebhart, 1988), but also involved in pain facilitatory processes (Vanegas and Schaible, 2004) which makes it a key structure of anti- as well as pro-nociceptive effects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The PAG is involved in pain facilitatory processes.
source: The PAG is not only known to mediate pain inhibition (Jones and Gebhart, 1988), but also involved in pain facilitatory processes (Vanegas and Schaible, 2004) which makes it a key structure of anti- as well as pro-nociceptive effects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The PAG is a key structure of anti- as well as pro-nociceptive effects.
source: The PAG is not only known to mediate pain inhibition (Jones and Gebhart, 1988), but also involved in pain facilitatory processes (Vanegas and Schaible, 2004) which makes it a key structure of anti- as well as pro-nociceptive effects.
evidence: This is an inference from cited prior research.

claim: Pain modulation underlying placebo hypoalgesia depends on the precision of the prior expectation.
source: Our behavioral data shows that pain modulation underlying placebo hypoalgesia depends on the precision of the prior expectation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: The PAG is an area crucially involved in precision biased integration processes due to its opposing modulatory properties.
source: Therefore, our data suggests that the PAG is an area crucially involved in precision biased integration processes due to its opposing modulatory properties.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining behavioral and fMRI findings with prior knowledge.

claim: Previous research observed a representation of uncertainty in the PAG during a painful vicarious observation task.
source: Previous research already hinted at a representation of uncertainty in the PAG during a painful vicarious observation task (Yoshida et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Yoshida et al. observed a potent hyperalgesia effect during vicarious observation task in subjects who showed high susceptibility to induced variability and related this to an increased BOLD signal in the PAG.
source: They observed a potent hyperalgesia effect during this vicarious observation task in subjects who showed high susceptibility to induced variability and related this to an increased BOLD signal in the periaqueductal gray (PAG).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited prior study.

claim: The data indicates a significant influence of the PAG in variability coding.
source: By using an optimally integrated precision weight to explicitly investigate the influence of variability irrespective of the mean intensity of pain in the placebo treatment context, our data indicates a significant influence of the PAG in variability coding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: Facilitatory as well as inhibitory projections from the PAG relay in the RVM.
source: We additionally observed that the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) is involved in this process. Again, facilitatory as well as inhibitory projections from the PAG relay in the RVM (Vanegas and Schaible, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In both PAG and RVM, a stronger activation was observed when the treatment expectation was less precise (i.e. high variability) relative to the precision of the incoming sensory stimuli.
source: In both, PAG and RVM, a stronger activation was observed when the treatment expectation was less precise (i.e. high variability) relative to the precision of the incoming sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings.

claim: The placebo effect literature reports PAG activation patterns being both increased or decreased in placebo hypoalgesia reflecting the mediating effect of this area.
source: Dependent on the context, including anticipatory and/or direct responses to nociceptive stimuli, the placebo effect literature reports PAG activation patterns being both, increased or decreased in placebo hypoalgesia reflecting the mediating effect of this area (Eippert et al., 2009; Geuter et al., 2013; Peciña et al., 2013; Scott et al., 2008; Wager et al., 2004; Wager et al., 2007; Wager and Atlas, 2015; Zubieta et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The RVM shows mainly increased activation in placebo hypoalgesia.
source: whereas the RVM shows mainly increased activation in placebo hypoalgesia (Eippert et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: These activation patterns are likely being related to variability coding.
source: These activation patterns are likely being related to variability coding as seen in our results.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting prior findings to the current results.

claim: Variability during pain most probably introduces uncertainty about future painfulness.
source: Variability during pain most probably introduces uncertainty about future painfulness (Seidel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Less precise prior treatment expectations based on missing information lead to higher activation in the PAG probably due to processing less predictable outcomes.
source: In this context, our data suggests that less precise prior treatment expectations based on missing information lead to higher activation in the PAG probably due to processing less predictable (Fairhurst et al., 2007) outcomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings supported by a citation.

claim: The PAG's modulatory processing is reflected by signal increase in the presence of non-precise information about a treatment.
source: It seems that the PAG's modulatory processing (Jones and Gebhart, 1988; Linnman et al., 2012; Vanegas and Schaible, 2004) is reflected by this signal increase in the presence of non-precise information about a treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings supported by citations.

claim: Some studies showed that PAG placebo-induced signal increases were related to the strength of the analgesic effect connecting this to the opioidergic descending pain control system.
source: Also, some studies were able to show that PAG placebo-induced signal increases were related to the strength of the analgesic effect connecting this to the opioidergic descending pain control system (Eippert et al., 2009; Peciña et al., 2013; Wager et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PAG signal increase is related to less precise prior treatment expectations (prior) compared to more precise incoming sensory stimuli (likelihood) during a placebo treatment.
source: Our results additionally indicate that PAG signal increase is related to less precise prior treatment expectations (prior) compared to more precise incoming sensory stimuli (likelihood) during a placebo treatment, importantly not being related to simple pain intensity but rather optimally integrated variability coding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: An influence of prior treatment precision levels on opioidergic descending pain modulations is speculated.
source: Therefore, an influence of prior treatment precision levels on opioidergic descending pain modulations is speculated as we also observed the same trend-wise activation pattern in the RVM.
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and prior knowledge.

claim: The anticipated analgesic effect was positively correlated with a signal increase in the PAG, reflecting the responsiveness of this brainstem area to placebo-induced expectations.
source: This is supported by a previous finding of the anticipated analgesic effect being positively correlated with a signal increase in the PAG (Scott et al., 2008), reflecting the responsiveness of this brainstem area to placebo-induced expectations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In both PAG and RVM, placebo-induced BOLD-activations can be significantly reduced by naloxone.
source: In both areas, PAG and RVM, placebo-induced BOLD-activations can be significantly reduced by naloxone (Eippert et al., 2009), an opioid-antagonist known to impair placebo-dependent pain reduction (Amanzio and Benedetti, 1999; Grevert et al., 1983; Levine and Gordon, 1984; Levine, 1978), which reflects their involvement in the opioidergic descending pain control system.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: An involvement of the opioidergic descending pain system is likely.
source: As these are the two brain regions we also observed during the coding of expectation precision under a placebo treatment condition, an involvement of the opioidergic descending pain system is likely.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior knowledge about opioidergic systems.
